extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of moral/political philosophy, legislators, judges, and social scientists
extracted.subtask_short: logic of practice for ethics and policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming and applying practical rules (art, policy, and morality) grounded in scientific/theoretical knowledge, and for interpreting social/historical causal claims. Targets legislators, judges, moralists, and social scientists who must convert theory into precepts or evaluate historical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statistical aggregates to verify social causal laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical regularities observed en masse (e.g., nearly constant proportions of murders, suicides, accidents, undirected letters) provide a posteriori verification of causal laws in human conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large numbers and careful recordation yield surprising regularity despite individual irregularity; use wide fields and sufficient sample sizes to eliminate chance and reveal general causes. Examples: constancy of murder rates, comparative instruments used, ratio of legitimate/illegitimate births, and post-office data on undirected letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish general causes from special (individual) causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Every human action is the concurrent result of general circumstances (moral, educational, economic influences) and special individual causes (temperament, parentage, associates). Aggregates show the net effect of general causes when the observation field includes all combinations of special causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing social phenomena, separate effects of broad societal influences from idiosyncratic individual influences; the collective experiment 'exactly separates' these and reveals what is attributable to general causes. Do not conflate the two when inferring explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer determinism of individual acts from aggregate regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularity of aggregate results does not imply each particular event (e.g., each murder) is caused solely by general causes or that individual choice is illusory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the corollary that one person's abstention would simply be 'made up' by another to preserve averages. Recognize that special causes can be more powerful than general ones for individual acts even if they average out in large samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware drawing broad moral conclusions from narrow statistical fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences (e.g., that moral qualities are scarcely improvable or unimportant) drawn from statistics compiled within narrow geographical limits or short successive years are unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such statistics eliminate moral causes except those common to the region/time. To assess moral influence, compare across ages, countries, or regions differing in moral elements; do not generalize from narrow samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate causation from fatalism; preserve agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of universal causal laws does not imply fatalism. Human volitions are among the causes and can be efficacious; believing in causes is not the same as denying the power of human effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that average outcomes may themselves depend on average human efforts (e.g., shipwreck survival). Treat causation as compatible with effective human action and modification of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the decisive role of exceptional individuals and governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptional individuals (great men) and governments can be indispensable links in chains of causation, affecting celerity and sometimes the very occurrence of progress; their influence need not be neutralized by averaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss the historical efficacy of great persons/governments. Their actions can determine the speed, order, or even possibility of developments (examples: Newton, Socrates, Mohammed, Themistocles, Spanish 18th-century reforms). Historical explanation should allow for such singular causal agents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical science yields conditional, not absolute, predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because contingent combinations of exceptional persons and circumstances matter, historical science can only authorize conditional and approximate generalizations about future developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictions should be qualified by the limits of available averages and by the unpredictable effects of rare but potent events or persons; emphasize conditionality in prognostications about social evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different duties for judge versus legislator (rule application vs rule-formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judge, under a definite code, must apply pre-established law by ratiocination (syllogism) without re-questioning the law's reasons; a legislator must examine the reasons and grounds of maxims and consider the scientific/theoretical bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat rule-formation and rule-application as identical tasks; practitioners who follow rules without understanding their reasons (the 'slave of formulas') are rightly criticized. When forming policy, inquire into the scientific theorems that justify precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art (practical rules) must be grounded in completed scientific knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A theorem or speculative truth is not ripe to be turned into a precept until the whole scientific process has been performed, including negative conditions that would prevent the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rules are framed on incomplete theory (missing counteracting causes), they will fail when overlooked contingencies occur. To form reliable precepts, finish the theoretical investigation of all conditions influencing the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept practical rules as provisional and context-limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of art are necessarily imperfect for convenience: they cover the most numerous or ordinary cases and omit rare contingencies to remain apprehensible and usable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use common rules as provisional guidance when time/resources preclude full analysis; yet, where possible, revert to scientific principles and adjust the rule to particular circumstances. Expect rules to be modified when exceptional circumstances arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance completeness and usability in rule formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Including all counteracting contingencies in a rule would make it too cumbrous to be apprehended and remembered; therefore rules omit some conditions and are simplified for ordinary use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rules to be manageable while knowing their limits. Train practitioners to recognize when omitted contingencies matter and to consult deeper theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deducing particular conduct solely from universal practical maxims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning downward from general practical maxims (without reference to their speculative grounds) is an error; practical maxims must rest on speculative/scientific grounds that justify them as means to desirable ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political geometrical school example: arguing that a measure ought to be adopted because it follows from a principle of government ignores trade-offs and practical contingencies. Always check the theoretical bases and possible conflicts of ends before applying a maxim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for conflicts of ends when applying rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that the success of a rule's prescribed means in attaining its end is unambiguously desirable; success may conflict with other ends that could be more desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before adopting a rule, consider whether achieving its targeted end might interfere with other values or objectives; weigh competing ends and the broader consequences of implementing the rule.
